deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a continuous prose passage in German Kurrent script from what look like lecture or school notes on ancient history: the campaign of Alexander the Great in Asia Minor in 334–333 BC. It continues the previous page (Battle of the Granicus) and runs into the next (Battle of Issus, siege of Tyre).

Content, restated:
(1) After the Granicus, Alexander defeated the Persians and advanced into Lydia.
(2) Memnon defended Ephesus. Driven out, he defended Halicarnassus (marginal insertion: 'die Stadt'), which cost Alexander a siege.
(3) Memnon then tried to take Macedonia. On the way he besieged Lesbos, but died (marked with the dagger sign †) before he could accomplish it.
(4) In summer 333 Alexander took Pamphylia, Pisidia and Phrygia, pushed to the Halys and went into Cilicia, where he fell gravely ill.
(5) Alexander marched along the coast. Darius and Alexander met at Issus. Alexander chose favourable ground, a plain surrounded by mountains; the sentence continues on the next page.

There is no derivation, computation or mathematical problem to reconstruct. The page is a historical narrative bound into a Gauss bundle; the hand and genre suggest student or family notes rather than Gauss's own research.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. Historical content is broadly accurate for a school-level summary. Memnon did die during operations on Lesbos (at the siege of Mytilene, 333 BC). Alexander did fall seriously ill in Cilicia (at Tarsus, after bathing in the Cydnus).
'drang bis an den Halys' is a simplification: Alexander's route went through Gordium in Phrygia, and he did not campaign along the Halys in any substantial way.
The order is compressed: the Pamphylia/Pisidia campaign fell in winter 334/333 BC, before the summer of 333.
deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical: a routine historical narrative on Alexander the Great's Asia Minor campaign, apparently from lecture or school notes. It contains no mathematical content attributable to Gauss.
transcription_corrections: Line 2–3: 'ver-/verdrängt' is a line-break duplication; read 'verdrängt'.
Line 5: 'Memnon setzte sich nun um sich Macedoniens zu bemächtigen' more plausibly reads 'Memnon suchte sich nun auch Macedoniens zu bemächtigen'.
Line 6: 'bei diesem aber †er[?]' — the dagger is the conventional death sign, so read 'bei diesem aber starb (†) er, ehe er zu Stande kam'.
The first † before 'Halikarnassus' is an insertion mark keyed to the marginal 'die Stadt'; it is not a death sign.
'Bei Issus[?]': the reading 'Issus' is confirmed by context and by the next page's battle description.
'treffen' is as written; it may be intended as 'trafen'.
